summary: Describes how to handle internationalized email when a server along the path cannot cope with UTF-8 in addresses and headers, instead of rejecting the message. It defines a downgrading mechanism for the experimental UTF8SMTP extension. It was replaced by RFC 6530.

eli5.summary: Some mail servers only understand plain English letters. This note describes how to convert a message with other alphabets so it can still travel through them, rather than being thrown away.

questions: how do internationalized emails work with legacy mail servers
subtitle: Converting internationalized emails to ASCII when crossing non-UTF8-capable mail servers

tldr.problem: Mail servers in the delivery path may not support UTF-8 in addresses and headers, causing internationalized messages to be rejected instead of delivered.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5504 defines a downgrading process that converts UTF-8 addresses and headers to ASCII-safe representations while preserving the original information in new header fields starting with 'Downgraded-'.
tldr.outcome: This allows internationalized messages to transit through legacy mail systems, with the original information preserved for systems that understand it. It was replaced by RFC 6530 with a more complete specification.

today: RFC 5504 is Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 6530. Modern systems implementing email internationalization should use RFC 6530 instead of this experimental specification.

sections.title: The Downgrading Problem
sections.content:
The Email Address Internationalization (EAI) specifications (RFC 4952, RFC 5335, RFC 5336) enable UTF-8 in email addresses and headers. However, not all mail servers support this capability. If a message with UTF-8 addresses reaches a non-UTF8SMTP-compliant server, that server will reject the message entirely rather than deliver it to its destination.

RFC 5504 solves this by defining a downgrading mechanism: the conversion of internationalized envelopes and headers to all-ASCII representations that can be safely processed by legacy systems. The key insight is that downgrading is one-way and lossy—the original UTF-8 information is preserved in new header fields but cannot be perfectly reconstructed.

Downgrading may occur in Mail User Agents (MUAs), Mail Submission Agents (MSAs), Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs), Message Delivery Agents (MDAs), POP servers, and IMAP servers whenever an internationalized message must cross a non-UTF8SMTP system.
sections.eli5: When a message with foreign alphabets encounters a mail server that doesn't understand them, this process converts those letters to ASCII so the server accepts it. The original letters are saved in special header fields in case a newer server later reads the message.

sections.title: The Downgrading Approach
sections.content:
RFC 5504 defines downgrading in four parts:

  • New header fields: Fields starting with 'Downgraded-' preserve original UTF-8 values from the envelope and headers. For example, 'Downgraded-From:' saves the original UTF-8 sender address.
  • SMTP downgrading: The envelope addresses (MAIL FROM and RCPT TO commands) are converted to ASCII. When a non-ASCII address has an alternative ASCII address (provided via the ALT-ADDRESS parameter in RFC 5336), that ASCII version is used.
  • Header field downgrading: Each header field containing non-ASCII characters is converted to ASCII using appropriate encoding methods.
  • MIME body-part downgrading: The same conversion is applied to header fields in MIME body parts.

The result is a message compliant with RFC 5321 (SMTP) and RFC 5322 (message format) that can be transmitted through any mail system, while the original information remains retrievable.
sections.eli5: The method works in four steps: save the original addresses and headers in special fields, convert the envelope addresses to English, convert the header fields to English, and convert the MIME part headers too. Afterward, older mail servers can handle the message.

sections.title: Preservation Header Fields
sections.content:
RFC 5504 introduces new header fields to preserve information that would otherwise be lost during downgrading.

Envelope downgrading fields: 'Downgraded-Mail-From:' and 'Downgraded-Rcpt-To:' preserve the original non-ASCII envelope addresses. The format includes both the original UTF-8 address and the ASCII downgraded version, so a system reading this header can recover the original information.

Address header fields: For headers containing addresses (From, To, Cc, Bcc, Reply-To, Sender, Return-Path, and others), a corresponding 'Downgraded-' header is added to preserve the original UTF-8 content. These fields are RFC 2047-encoded so they remain ASCII-safe while storing UTF-8 text.

Unknown header fields: Custom headers containing non-ASCII characters are preserved in 'Downgraded-' versions of themselves, with RFC 2047 encoding applied.

A security note: to prevent unintended disclosure of recipient addresses in messages with multiple recipients, 'Downgraded-Rcpt-To:' is not added when there are multiple recipients.
sections.eli5: New header fields save the original non-English addresses and text. These fields use a standard encoding so mail systems can read them even though they contain the original letters.

sections.title: Downgrading Methods by Field Type
sections.content:
RFC 5504 specifies different downgrading strategies for different types of header fields:

  • UNSTRUCTURED fields (Subject, Comments): Apply RFC 2047 encoding to any non-ASCII text.
  • WORD fields (Keywords): Apply RFC 2047 encoding.
  • COMMENT fields (any field with parenthetical comments): Apply RFC 2047 encoding to the comment content.
  • MIME-VALUE fields (Content-Type, Content-Disposition parameters): Use RFC 2231 parameter encoding with UTF-8 charset.
  • DISPLAY-NAME fields (the display name in address headers): Apply RFC 2047 encoding.
  • MAILBOX fields (email addresses in To, From, etc.): If the address has an ASCII alternative from the ALT-ADDRESS parameter, use it. Otherwise, preserve the original in a 'Downgraded-' field and replace the address with a marker.
  • Received header: Remove the 'FOR' clause if it contains a non-ASCII address.

These different methods balance the need to preserve information with the requirement to produce ASCII-only output that legacy systems can handle.
sections.eli5: Different types of headers need different conversion methods. Some use a standard encoding format, some just encode the addresses with a backup version. The Received header gets simplified by removing international addresses from it.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 5504 discusses implementation challenges. RFC 2047 encoding has known issues with whitespace handling in some deployed systems, so implementers may need to work around buggy implementations. The RFC allows for longer encoded words to accommodate this.

Trivial downgrading: Full downgrading is complex. The RFC defines a simpler 'trivial downgrading' for systems that cannot implement the full specification. This covers only simple subjects, comments, and display names, and only works for messages without non-ASCII email addresses. It is easier to implement but covers fewer cases.

7-bit transport: When encountering SMTP servers that do not support the 8BITMIME extension, implementers must convert 8-bit data to base64 or quoted-printable encoding and adjust the Content-Transfer-Encoding header accordingly.

Downgrading also breaks digital signatures (DKIM, S/MIME, OpenPGP) because the message content changes. This is unavoidable when crossing non-UTF8SMTP systems; the best mitigation is to use UTF8SMTP end-to-end when signatures are needed.
sections.eli5: Implementers need to handle quirks in email software, can choose between full or simplified conversion, and should know that downgrading breaks digital signatures. If signatures matter, use only UTF8-capable servers.
